beats.intro: Chapter seven, lesson seven: bulk transport. [[amoeba]]An amoeba hunting in a pond meets a bacterium much too big to slip through any channel or carrier. [[cell]]So how does it get the meal inside? [[patch]]Back at our patch of membrane, with the vesicles lit: small things cross through the bilayer or through proteins. Large molecules and whole particles travel in bulk, wrapped inside vesicles.
beats.bulk: Think of the difference between a checkpoint and a delivery truck. [[small]]Water, ions and small molecules pass one at a time, by the routes of the last lessons. [[big]]Proteins, polysaccharides, even bacteria are far too large for that. [[vesicle]]They ride in a vesicle, a bubble of membrane, and the membrane itself opens and closes around them. [[energy]]Unlike diffusion, this takes energy. The cell has to spend A T P to move vesicles, and to bend and fuse the membrane. So bulk transport is a kind of active transport.
beats.exo: First, out. [[move]]In exocytosis, a transport vesicle, loaded with product, migrates to the plasma membrane. [[fuse]]Its membrane fuses with the plasma membrane. [[release]]And the contents spill out of the cell. [[grow]]The vesicle's membrane becomes part of the plasma membrane, so the cell surface grows a little. [[secrete]]Many secretory cells export their products this way. A cell in the pancreas that releases the hormone insulin is one example, and a gland cell that releases digestive enzymes is another.
beats.q1: Quick check. Put the steps of exocytosis in order.
beats.endo: Now, in. [[in]]Endocytosis is the reverse. The cell takes in large molecules by forming vesicles from its own plasma membrane. [[rev]]The direction is reversed, and the machinery involves different proteins. [[three]]There are three kinds. Phagocytosis, cellular eating. Pinocytosis, cellular drinking. And receptor-mediated endocytosis.
beats.phago: Phagocytosis first. [[reach]]The amoeba reaches out with extensions called pseudopodia, which wrap around the bacterium. [[close]]They close up, and the particle ends up inside a food vacuole. [[lyso]]Next, a lysosome fuses with the food vacuole. Its digestive enzymes break the particle down, and the useful small molecules leave into the cytoplasm.
beats.pino: Pinocytosis is much less picky. [[dimple]]The membrane dimples inward at many places, [[gulp]]and pinches off tiny vesicles full of extracellular fluid. [[take]]Whatever happens to be dissolved in that fluid comes along. The cell does not choose its contents. It just gulps.
beats.rme: The third kind is selective. [[rec]]Receptor-mediated endocytosis starts with receptors, proteins in the membrane that fit one particular molecule. Any molecule that binds specifically to the receptor site of another molecule is called a ligand. [[bind]]When ligands bind their receptors, [[pit]]the membrane region sinks in and a coat of protein lines it. This is a coated pit. [[ves]]It pinches off as a coated vesicle, carrying the ligands inside. [[fluid]]Some fluid comes along as well, so even this route is not perfectly selective, but the receptors let the cell pick up its chosen molecules in large amounts.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which kind of endocytosis is it?
beats.recap: Let's finish with every way across the membrane in this chapter. [[w1]]Small nonpolar molecules, like oxygen, slip through the bilayer by simple diffusion, down their gradient. Water follows its own gradient by osmosis. [[w2]]Ions and polar molecules go through channels and carriers, which is facilitated diffusion. Still passive. [[w3]]To move against a gradient, a pump spends ATP, like the sodium-potassium pump. [[w4]]Cotransport lets the downhill flow of one solute drag another one uphill, like sucrose with hydrogen ions. [[w5]]And for big cargo, exocytosis sends vesicles out, and endocytosis brings them in. [[end]]Now try the practice.
